generatedSlides.title: EC2 selection: match the family to the bottleneck
generatedSlides.layout: Six distinct dimensional resource icons arranged around a workload lens, with six concise readable cards.
copy: C • Compute optimized
CPU-heavy applications, simulations and compute-intensive processing.
R • Memory optimized
Large working sets, in-memory databases and caches.
M • General purpose
Balanced CPU and memory for many application and web tiers.
I • Storage optimized
High local I/O for suitable databases and data processing; local disks need a durability plan.
G / P • Accelerated computing
GPU workloads such as graphics, rendering, ML training or inference; check the required accelerator.
T • Burstable
Variable CPU demand with a baseline and credit model; sustained demand can change performance or cost.
Validate the whole instance
Check vCPU, RAM, architecture, EBS bandwidth, network throughput and packet rate. Benchmark representative traffic.
Remember: Family letters guide selection; measured workload behavior proves the fit.

generatedSlides.title: Burstable compute and Graviton: two separate decisions
generatedSlides.layout: Preserve credit/CPU metaphor on left, an elegant Arm64 compatibility checklist on right; avoid quantitative charts.
copy: CPU credits
Earn credits below baseline; spend them above baseline. Standard mode is constrained when credits run out.
Unlimited mode
Sustained surplus-credit use can incur charges. Monitor credit balance and sustained CPU demand, not only a brief spike.
Graviton is Arm64
Use a supported Linux OS and Arm64 AMI. EC2 Graviton does not support Windows.
Check the software stack
Rebuild or select compatible binaries, container images and native libraries. Test agents, drivers and commercial software too.
Choose by workload
Web services, caches, HPC and encoding may fit. Benchmark latency, throughput and total cost against a compatible x86 option.

generatedSlides.title: EC2 purchasing: discount, flexibility and capacity
generatedSlides.layout: Three illustrated purchase-choice columns plus a clearly separate capacity assurance ribbon, not a pricing chart.
copy: On-Demand and Spot
On-Demand avoids a long commitment. Spot uses spare capacity and requires interruption-tolerant design.
Savings Plans
Commit eligible usage spend for discounts. A discount commitment does not itself guarantee capacity.
Reserved Instances
Choose a 1-year or 3-year term. Standard offers a larger discount but cannot be exchanged; Convertible allows supported exchanges.
Payment choices
All Upfront, Partial Upfront or No Upfront. Higher upfront payment generally improves the discount; payment obligations remain even when unused.
Capacity is a separate question

Regional RIs provide a billing benefit without reserving capacity. Matching zonal RIs can provide capacity reservation; On-Demand Capacity Reservations reserve matching capacity and can incur idle charges.
Remember: Match commitment to stable demand, flexibility to expected change, and capacity assurance to availability requirements.

generatedSlides.title: Spot design: price does not promise capacity
generatedSlides.layout: Glossy interruption-ready worker illustration, durable checkpoint vault, diversified instance tiles and warning bell; four teaching stations.
copy: Why interruption happens
AWS can reclaim spare capacity; a configured price ceiling can also affect eligibility. A low price or accepted request does not guarantee future capacity.
Treat notices as best effort
The usual interruption warning is two minutes, but it is not guaranteed. Hibernation starts immediately without that two-minute lead.
Prepare the application
Use Spot for retryable batch, analytics or stateless work. Checkpoint to durable storage, drain when possible and make retries idempotent.
Diversify the supply
Use multiple suitable instance types and AZs with a capacity-aware allocation strategy. Capacity Rebalancing may start replacements early, but cannot guarantee capacity.
Separate the lifecycle actions
Canceling a Spot request and terminating a running instance are different operations; verify the intended request and instance state.
Remember: Savings are useful only when the workload can recover from interruption.

generatedSlides.title: Tenancy: isolation, licensing and host affinity
generatedSlides.layout: Three dimensional hardware islands for shared, Dedicated Instances and Dedicated Hosts, plus a host-affinity tag and recovery badge.
copy: Shared tenancy
Instances can run on hardware shared with other customers.
Dedicated Instances
Hardware is dedicated to your account, but you do not get host-level placement visibility or host affinity.
Dedicated Hosts
Allocate a physical server with host visibility and placement controls. Useful for eligible per-socket or per-core software licenses.
Host affinity
Bind an instance to a particular host for subsequent starts. Auto-placement allows eligible launches onto available compatible hosts.
Plan recovery and licensing
Supported host recovery can allocate a replacement host in the same AZ; recovered instances establish affinity with it. Validate license terms, software support, recovery eligibility and cost.
Remember: Dedicated hardware is an isolation choice; license compliance and recovery still require an explicit design.

generatedSlides.title: Placement groups: locality, isolation and operational limits
generatedSlides.layout: Three rich conceptual hardware vignettes, cluster, rack spread and partition replicas. No exact rack topology. A short operation ribbon below.
copy: Cluster • performance
Supported instances close together in one AZ for low latency and throughput. One rack is not guaranteed; the slower instance limits the pair.
Spread • small critical fleets
Rack-level spread separates underlying hardware: up to 7 running instances per AZ per group. It can span AZs; host-level spread is an Outposts option.
Partition • distributed replicas
Up to 7 partitions per AZ; different partitions do not share racks. Use partition metadata to place replicas across failure boundaries, as in Kafka, Cassandra or HDFS.
Change placement deliberately
Stop the instance, change placement with ModifyInstancePlacement, then start. Compatible capacity is required; launches or starts can fail when unavailable.
Remember: Placement controls locality or hardware separation. It does not create replication or Multi-AZ recovery.

generatedSlides.title: EC2 networking: ENA, EFA and the software stack
generatedSlides.layout: Two glossy network adapter metaphors with three labeled conceptual software-layer tiles, not a precise topology.
copy: ENA • enhanced networking
Hardware-assisted SR-IOV networking improves throughput, packet rate and CPU efficiency on supported instances. Check drivers and instance limits.
EFA • application communication
Low-latency inter-node communication for supported Linux HPC and ML workloads. Compatible MPI or NCCL stacks use libfabric and the appropriate EFA integration.
OS bypass needs prerequisites
Use supported instance types, software and same-AZ placement. Configure required security-group rules; EFA does not accelerate arbitrary unmodified software.
Legacy context
Intel 82599 VF is an older enhanced-networking option. Historical 10/100-Gbps examples are not universal caps for modern instances.
Remember: Match bandwidth, packet rate and latency to the workload; verify the application can use the selected networking stack.

generatedSlides.title: HPC: align compute, data movement and recovery
generatedSlides.layout: A dimensional scientific-computing workstation and independent task tiles, with three data-staging icons; not a quantitative chart or exact topology.
copy: Start with the job
Weather simulation and computational chemistry can need tightly coupled communication; rendering and independent analytics tasks scale differently.
Fit every layer
Choose CPU or GPU compute, placement and networking for communication needs. Storage must fit object, shared-file, block or disposable-scratch access.
Stage data before scaling
Direct Connect supplies a dedicated network path; add encryption where required. DataSync manages supported online transfers, including S3, EFS and FSx for Windows File Server.
Offline-transfer context
The reference PDF uses Snowball for very large offline transfers. Snowball Edge is available only to existing customers since November 7, 2025; validate eligibility and current alternatives.
Orchestrate and recover
Compare AWS Batch job scheduling with ParallelCluster cluster management. Plan checkpoints, data persistence, output collection and restart behavior.
Remember: Faster compute cannot compensate for slow staging, communication or storage.

generatedSlides.title: Target tracking: choose demand per unit of capacity
generatedSlides.layout: A target and balanced worker sculpture surrounded by four meaningful metric icons and short explanation panels. No plotted measurements.
copy: How the controller responds
Target tracking adjusts capacity to keep a suitable utilization metric near its target. Adding instances must reduce load per instance.
Match the metric
CPU for CPU-bound work; ALB requests per target for balanced request processing; average network bytes in or out for suitable network-bound workloads.
Custom metrics need useful units
A queue's raw length is not proportional utilization. Backlog per worker can express demand; choose the target from acceptable latency and processing time.
Coordinate readiness and policies
Allow instance warmup and verify scale-in. With multiple target tracking policies, any can request scale-out; all scale-in-enabled policies must agree before scale-in.
Remember: A scaling metric must describe the bottleneck that more healthy capacity can actually relieve.

generatedSlides.title: Health checks: identify the failure before replacement
generatedSlides.layout: Four glossy diagnostic instruments with meaningful icons for infrastructure, guest/storage, HTTP application and custom automation. No exact architecture diagram.
copy: EC2 managed checks
System checks assess underlying infrastructure; instance checks assess guest reachability. Attached EBS checks assess volume reachability and I/O capability.
Application checks
Configured HTTP/HTTPS criteria test application behavior. For an ASG, enable the intended health sources and set an appropriate grace period.
Custom ASG health
Your automation can report health through the CLI or SDK using SetInstanceHealth. Decide when a failure warrants replacing that instance.
Keep the endpoint useful
A shallow readiness check can detect a broken server. A database-dependent endpoint can mark the whole fleet unhealthy during one shared database outage.
Recovery is a different action
Supported EC2 recovery addresses certain system failures; ASG replacement creates new compute. Neither repairs every application or shared dependency.
Remember: A healthy guest is not proof of a healthy application. Choose the check and response for the failure domain.

generatedSlides.title: EC2 observability: know where each metric comes from
generatedSlides.layout: Glossy metric collector with five separate instrument cards, no charts or invented readings.
copy: CPU and credits
EC2 provides CPUUtilization. Burstable instances also expose credit usage and balances; inspect surplus-credit metrics for Unlimited mode.
Network
NetworkIn and NetworkOut show bytes; packet metrics help identify packet-rate pressure. Match the instance's bandwidth and packet limits.
Local disk versus EBS
DiskReadOps, DiskWriteOps and disk byte metrics describe instance-store I/O. Use appropriate EBS volume and supported Nitro EBS metrics for EBS behavior.
Inside the guest
Memory utilization and filesystem free space are not standard EC2 instance metrics. Install and configure CloudWatch agent or publish custom metrics.
Resolution and meaning
Basic monitoring is generally 5 minutes; detailed monitoring gives eligible EC2 metrics at 1 minute. Some metric families have their own cadence.
Remember: High CPU, storage I/O and low free memory are different signals. Inspect the right metric source before changing instance size.

generatedSlides.title: EC2 recovery: preserve identity, expect a restart
generatedSlides.layout: A glass instance identity card and attached-volume vault next to a restarted machine metaphor. Preserve/lost explanation columns, no exact state diagram.
copy: When recovery applies
Supported automatic recovery can address system-status-check failures. An instance-check failure alone does not trigger it.
What is preserved
Instance ID; public, private and Elastic IP addresses; metadata; placement group; attached EBS volumes; Availability Zone.
What is lost
RAM and OS uptime. With CloudWatch action-based recovery, instance-store data is also lost; verify the selected recovery mechanism and supported configuration.
Compare the alternatives
Stop/start can change an auto-assigned public IPv4 address. ASG replacement launches a different instance. Neither is identical to EC2 recovery.
Prepare before failure
Verify simplified automatic recovery or configure a supported CloudWatch recovery action. Monitor outcomes and keep backups and application recovery procedures.
Remember: Preserved identity does not preserve in-memory work or guarantee application recovery.

generatedSlides.title: HPC storage: choose the access pattern and durability
generatedSlides.layout: Five distinct polished storage objects with paired explanations, local scratch, block volume, object vault, shared folder and parallel files.
copy: Instance store • local scratch
Very low-latency local I/O, potentially millions of IOPS on suitable instances. Data is temporary; checkpoint valuable results elsewhere.
EBS • persistent block
Use compatible volume and instance limits. io2 Block Express supports up to 256,000 IOPS on supported configurations; provisioned performance still needs testing.
S3 • durable objects
Store datasets and results as objects. It is not a native POSIX filesystem; stage data or use a supported integration.
EFS • shared files
Managed NFS access for many clients. Throughput modes are Elastic, Provisioned and Bursting; throughput configuration is not provisioned IOPS.
FSx for Lustre • parallel I/O
A parallel filesystem for demanding HPC. S3 integration can stage datasets and export results; configure persistence and data movement deliberately.
Remember: Compute capacity, filesystem throughput, metadata access and durability must fit the same job.

generatedSlides.title: HPC orchestration: schedule jobs or provision a cluster?
generatedSlides.layout: Two dimensional conceptual workbenches: a managed job queue and a configurable cluster toolkit. A compact job-type example strip.
copy: AWS Batch
Submit jobs with resource requirements. Queues, scheduling and managed compute environments provision eligible capacity for execution.
Multi-node parallel jobs
One coordinated job spans multiple EC2 nodes. Use a supported managed environment and tightly coupled networking; these jobs do not support Spot or Fargate.
AWS ParallelCluster
AWS-supported open-source tooling provisions and manages HPC clusters from a configuration file, including compute, networking, scheduler and shared storage.
Choose the operating model
Batch fits managed job execution. ParallelCluster fits a configurable HPC cluster and supported scheduler workflow, such as Slurm.
Two workload shapes
Independent rendering tasks can retry separately. A multi-node MPI simulation requires coordinated nodes and suitable communication.
Remember: A scheduler, a cluster-provisioning tool and an application communication library solve different problems.

generatedSlides.title: Auto Scaling processes: nine controls with different jobs
generatedSlides.layout: A beautifully arranged nine-control instrument panel. Each control has an icon and readable one-sentence purpose; not a literal console or flowchart.
copy: Launch
Adds instances to the group.
Terminate
Removes instances from the group.
HealthCheck
Evaluates managed health checks and marks unhealthy instances.
ReplaceUnhealthy
Replaces instances marked unhealthy.
AZRebalance
Redistributes capacity across configured Availability Zones.
AlarmNotification
Responds to CloudWatch alarms for scaling policies.
ScheduledActions
Runs configured scheduled capacity changes.
AddToLoadBalancer
Registers new instances with the configured load balancer or target group.
InstanceRefresh
Replaces instances during a configured refresh.
Remember: Suspending one process does not suspend the entire group. Check which control actually causes the behavior.

generatedSlides.title: Suspended processes: diagnose the side effects
generatedSlides.layout: Four clearly differentiated operational case cards with dimmed control icons and small warning badges, not a console screenshot.
copy: Launch suspended
Scale-out cannot add instances. ReplaceUnhealthy can still terminate unhealthy instances without launching replacements.
ReplaceUnhealthy suspended
Managed health checks can still mark instances unhealthy, but replacement waits until the process resumes.
AddToLoadBalancer suspended
New instances can launch without registration. Resuming does not register those missed instances automatically; register them explicitly.
ScheduledActions suspended
Actions scheduled during the suspension are skipped. Resuming does not replay missed schedules.
Before resuming
Inspect capacity, health, registration and pending work. Resumption may trigger replacement or rebalancing; restore controls deliberately.
Remember: Suspending Terminate does not prevent the Spot service from interrupting Spot instances.

generatedSlides.title: Deployments: rolling replacement or parallel fleets?
generatedSlides.layout: Three original glossy deployment choice vignettes with versioned fleet miniatures, traffic dial and DNS card. Conceptual only, not a precise network topology.
copy: Rolling instance refresh
Replace instances within an ASG using a new launch-template version. Control healthy capacity and warmup; monitor and validate rollback support.
Parallel ASGs and target groups
Keep old and new fleets in separate groups. An ALB can shift traffic with weighted target groups; test the new version before increasing its share.
Separate load balancers and DNS
Expose each fleet through its own load balancer and use weighted Route 53 records for gradual cutover. DNS caching makes changes non-instantaneous.
Keep the test and rollback path
Use isolated test access or load tests before cutover. Plan sessions, schema compatibility, spare capacity and old-fleet retention.
Remember: Reverting traffic does not undo a database migration or recover lost application state.

generatedSlides.title: Spot Fleet: pools, target capacity and allocation
generatedSlides.layout: Dimensional fleet request envelope surrounded by diverse compute pools and four allocation-choice cards. No price chart or invented discount percentages.
copy: Define the fleet
Request target capacity across eligible instance-type, OS and AZ pools, with Spot and optional On-Demand instances. Weights can express useful capacity units.
priceCapacityOptimized
Select high-availability capacity pools, then consider price; the recommended choice for most Spot workloads.
capacityOptimized
Prioritize pools with stronger capacity availability to reduce near-term interruption risk.
diversified
Distribute Spot capacity across the specified pools.
lowestPrice
Prioritize low-price pools; generally not recommended because interruption risk is higher.
Choose the fleet manager too
Spot Fleet is distinct from an ASG mixed-instances policy. EC2 Auto Scaling generally offers richer ongoing fleet-management features.
Remember: Target capacity is a request, not a guarantee. Pool selection never removes interruption risk.

generatedSlides.title: Solution architecture: place compute in the whole system
generatedSlides.layout: An original conceptual architecture bookshelf: eight beautifully illustrated layers with readable service examples. No arrows or exact network topology; no official logo imitation.
copy: DNS and delivery
Route 53 resolves names; CloudFront brings cacheable content closer to users.
Application ingress
ALB, NLB and API Gateway handle different ingress needs; an Elastic IP is an address, not a load balancer.
Compute
EC2 and Auto Scaling, Lambda, ECS, EKS, Fargate, Batch and EMR provide different execution models.
Sessions and caching
ElastiCache and DynamoDB DAX reduce repeated access where their consistency and data models fit.
Data services
RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, OpenSearch and Redshift serve different transactional, search and analytical needs.
Messaging and workflows
SQS, SNS, Kinesis, Amazon MQ and Step Functions decouple work, move events or coordinate steps.
Storage and static assets
S3 and S3 Glacier classes, EBS, EFS and instance store have different access and durability models.
Remember: Choose each layer for its responsibility, then validate dependencies, security, cost and failure behavior across the system.

Batch fits managed job execution. ParallelCluster fits a configurable HPC cluster and supported scheduler workflow, such as Slurm.
Two workload shapes
Independent rendering tasks can retry separately. A multi-node MPI simulation requires coordinated nodes and suitable communication.
Remember: A scheduler, a cluster-provisioning tool and an application communication library solve different problems.

desiredFinalCopy.title: Auto Scaling processes: nine controls with different jobs
desiredFinalCopy.layout: A beautifully arranged nine-control instrument panel. Each control has an icon and readable one-sentence purpose; not a literal console or flowchart.
copy: Launch
Adds instances to the group.
Terminate
Removes instances from the group.
HealthCheck
Evaluates managed health checks and marks unhealthy instances.
ReplaceUnhealthy
Replaces instances marked unhealthy.
AZRebalance
Redistributes capacity across configured Availability Zones.
AlarmNotification
Responds to CloudWatch alarms for scaling policies.
ScheduledActions
Runs configured scheduled capacity changes.
AddToLoadBalancer
Registers new instances with the configured load balancer or target group.
InstanceRefresh
Replaces instances during a configured refresh.
Remember: Suspending one process does not suspend the entire group. Check which control actually causes the behavior.

desiredFinalCopy.title: Suspended processes: diagnose the side effects
desiredFinalCopy.layout: Four clearly differentiated operational case cards with dimmed control icons and small warning badges, not a console screenshot.
copy: Launch suspended
Scale-out cannot add instances. ReplaceUnhealthy can still terminate unhealthy instances without launching replacements.
ReplaceUnhealthy suspended
Managed health checks can still mark instances unhealthy, but replacement waits until the process resumes.
AddToLoadBalancer suspended
New instances can launch without registration. Resuming does not register those missed instances automatically; register them explicitly.
ScheduledActions suspended
Actions scheduled during the suspension are skipped. Resuming does not replay missed schedules.
Before resuming
Inspect capacity, health, registration and pending work. Resumption may trigger replacement or rebalancing; restore controls deliberately.
Remember: Suspending Terminate does not prevent the Spot service from interrupting Spot instances.

desiredFinalCopy.title: Deployments: rolling replacement or parallel fleets?
desiredFinalCopy.layout: Three original glossy deployment choice vignettes with versioned fleet miniatures, traffic dial and DNS card. Conceptual only, not a precise network topology.
copy: Rolling instance refresh
Replace instances within an ASG using a new launch-template version. Control healthy capacity and warmup; monitor and validate rollback support.
Parallel ASGs and target groups
Keep old and new fleets in separate groups. An ALB can shift traffic with weighted target groups; test the new version before increasing its share.
Separate load balancers and DNS
Expose each fleet through its own load balancer and use weighted Route 53 records for gradual cutover. DNS caching makes changes non-instantaneous.
Keep the test and rollback path
Use isolated test access or load tests before cutover. Plan sessions, schema compatibility, spare capacity and old-fleet retention.
Remember: Reverting traffic does not undo a database migration or recover lost application state.

desiredFinalCopy.title: Spot Fleet: pools, target capacity and allocation
desiredFinalCopy.layout: Dimensional fleet request envelope surrounded by diverse compute pools and four allocation-choice cards. No price chart or invented discount percentages.
copy: Define the fleet
Target capacity can combine Spot and optional On-Demand. Define pools by instance type, OS and AZ; weights express useful capacity units. Price or budget constraints can prevent fulfillment.
priceCapacityOptimized
Select high-availability capacity pools, then consider price; the recommended choice for most Spot workloads.
capacityOptimized
Prioritize pools with stronger capacity availability to reduce near-term interruption risk.
diversified
Distribute Spot capacity across the specified pools.
lowestPrice
Prioritize low-price pools; generally not recommended because interruption risk is higher.
Choose the fleet manager too
Spot Fleet is distinct from an ASG mixed-instances policy. EC2 Auto Scaling generally offers richer ongoing fleet-management features.
Remember: Target capacity is a request, not a guarantee. Pool selection never removes interruption risk.

desiredFinalCopy.title: Solution architecture: place compute in the whole system
desiredFinalCopy.layout: An original conceptual architecture bookshelf: eight beautifully illustrated layers with readable service examples. No arrows or exact network topology; no official logo imitation.
copy: DNS and delivery
Route 53 resolves names; CloudFront brings cacheable content closer to users.
Application ingress
ALB, NLB and API Gateway handle different ingress needs; an Elastic IP is an address, not a load balancer.
Compute
EC2 and Auto Scaling, Lambda, ECS, EKS, Fargate, Batch and EMR provide different execution models.
Sessions and caching
ElastiCache and DynamoDB DAX reduce repeated access where their consistency and data models fit.
Data services
RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, OpenSearch and Redshift serve different transactional, search and analytical needs.
Messaging and workflows
SQS, SNS, Kinesis, Amazon MQ and Step Functions decouple work, move events or coordinate steps.
Storage and static assets
S3 and S3 Glacier classes, EBS, EFS and instance store have different access and durability models.
Remember: Choose each layer for its responsibility, then validate dependencies, security, cost and failure behavior across the system.
